notes.note: Tempos match and the keys are neighbours: take a long 32-bar blend and swap the bass halfway through.
Same key, same tempo. Layer the percussion in early and let the new groove lift the floor a notch.
A small nudge on the pitch fader, then a steady blend; bring the new track in over the outgoing drums.
No pitch change needed. Hold both for a full phrase, then cut the old bass as the new one lands.
Barely a tempo change and the same key: an easy place for a long, lazy blend.
Neighbouring keys at matched tempo. Bring it in underneath and open the filter as the energy steps up.
Same key and nearly the same speed; tease the new hook in early and ride the two together.
Pitch it up a touch before you start, then blend on the drums and swap bass lines at the phrase change.
Tempos are locked and the keys are neighbours. Keep the blend tight and let the new track do the lifting.
Same key, slightly quicker. Ease the pitch up during a quiet passage so nobody feels the tempo move.
Matched in key, tempo and energy: this is the one to loop and layer for as long as you like.
Relative major, so the notes agree and the mood brightens. Time the swap for the high point of the set.
Neighbouring keys, same tempo. You are coming off the peak, so take a longer blend and let it settle.
Relative minor: the notes agree but the mood darkens. Bring the pitch down a little and blend slowly.
Same key and a hair slower. A relaxed blend to start bringing the room down for the close.
